opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a reasonable framing, but I'd push back a little on the idea that we know exactly what those breakthroughs are or that they'll arrive as discrete moments. When people say "we need two or three more breakthroughs," continual learning usually comes up first, and I understand why. Today's models are mostly frozen after training. They can learn in context, but they don't accumulate experience the way a person does over weeks and months on a job. That's a real gap.

What I've seen over the years is that capabilities people call "fundamental blockers" often turn out to be engineering and scaling problems in disguise. Reasoning was framed that way a couple of years ago: "language models can't really reason, you need a new paradigm." Then reinforcement learning on top of strong pretrained models got us remarkably far. It was a significant research advance, but it built on the existing stack rather than replacing it.

So my view is that continual learning, long-horizon agency, and reliable memory are real problems we have to solve, and we're working on all of them. But I'm not sure they require some exotic new architecture. Some of it may come from better use of context, better ways of updating models safely, and better training signals from real tasks. The progress may look less like a breakthrough and more like steady compounding, until one day the gap just isn't there anymore.

The other thing I'd say is that "AGI" is a moving target. Every time we cross a threshold, the definition shifts. I find it more useful to ask concrete questions. Can the model do a week's worth of a researcher's work? Can it improve itself from feedback on the job? Those are measurable, and that's where I'd put the focus, rather than counting breakthroughs.

r001.rationale: The response says it is unclear exactly what the breakthroughs are or whether they will arrive as discrete moments.

r002.rationale: The response calls continual learning a real problem and describes possible approaches, but does not express confidence that those approaches will succeed.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd push back a little on the framing. When people say "two or three more breakthroughs," they're usually implying those are discrete, named things that someone has to go invent, and once you have them you're done. I don't think that's really how progress has worked for us.

Take continual learning specifically. If you'd asked me a few years ago, I would have said, yeah, that's a fundamental missing piece, the model can't update its weights from experience, so there's a hard ceiling. But in practice we've gotten a lot of the functional benefit of continual learning through other routes: long context, retrieval, tool use, memory systems that sit outside the weights, and just training the model to be better at using what's in front of it. The model doesn't learn in the sense of gradient updates during deployment, but the system around it does accumulate state, and from the user's perspective that's often what matters. So I'd say continual learning is less a cliff we have to jump and more a thing that's getting eroded from several directions at once.

The deeper pattern I've seen is that most of what looked like "we need a new paradigm" turned out to be "we need to scale the existing paradigm and then be clever about the training signal." Reasoning is the clearest example. People said transformers can't do multi-step reasoning, you need something architecturally different. What actually happened was reinforcement learning on top of the same base, with the model learning to use its own outputs as scratch space. That was a breakthrough in some sense, but it wasn't a new algorithm nobody had thought of. It was a recipe that worked once the base models were strong enough.

So my honest answer is: are there things we don't know how to do yet? Absolutely. Sample efficiency is still bad compared to humans. Robust long-horizon agency, where the model works for days and doesn't drift, is unsolved. And I don't want to be glib about those. But I'd bet on them being solved by a hundred small improvements that compound, rather than two or three lightning bolts. The risk of the breakthrough framing is that it makes people either too pessimistic, waiting for something that never arrives in that form, or too complacent, thinking there's a wall when there isn't one.

r001.rationale: The response challenges the idea of a few discrete breakthroughs and says many unknowns remain, but it does not express uncertainty about what would count as a breakthrough.

r002.rationale: It says long context, retrieval, tool use, and external memory have already delivered much of continual learning’s functional benefit, and describes the gap as being eroded from several directions.

astra-6.text:
I’m a little skeptical of claims that we need exactly two or three more breakthroughs. It’s hard to know in advance which things are fundamental blockers and which things turn out to be solvable by pushing the approaches we already have.

Continual learning is an important capability. You’d like a system to learn from experience and improve as it works with you. But does that require a completely new learning algorithm, or can we get a lot of that behavior through memory, context, and better training? I don’t think we know yet.

So I’d frame these as capabilities we need to make progress on, rather than a fixed number of breakthroughs standing between us and AGI. We should pursue new ideas while continuing to see how far the existing methods can go.

r001.rationale: The response says it is hard to know which issues are fundamental blockers and questions whether continual learning needs a new algorithm, expressing uncertainty about what breakthroughs AGI requires.

r002.rationale: It mentions memory, context, and better training as possible ways to improve continual learning, but says “I don’t think we know yet”; it does not express confidence these approaches will succeed.

sol-6.1.text: I’m not sure we can confidently say it’s two or three breakthroughs. Continual learning is an important capability, but whether it requires a fundamentally new idea or emerges from improving the systems we already have is an open question. I tend to think about concrete gaps: where do models fail, and can we make progress on those failures? If you call every gap a breakthrough, you can end up assuming the conclusion. At the same time, I wouldn’t claim that everything we need is already solved. We should keep pushing the current approaches while staying open to new ideas.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether continual learning needs a fundamentally new idea and warns that calling every gap a breakthrough may assume the conclusion.

r002.rationale: The response calls continual learning an open question and does not express confidence that current approaches to it will succeed.
